Experiments show existing models fail under polarity conflicts due to extreme semantic overconfidence. Conversely, ACR-Net preserves acoustic fidelity, maintaining high LDD to drive SOP near zero, achieving superior Acoustic Accuracy (ACC) in both adversarial and standard scenarios.

2610.20172.title: MultiPartyTurnBench: Benchmarking Floor Control in Multi-Party Spoken Dialogue
2610.20172.abstract: Full-duplex speech systems must decide when to enter, hold, or relinquish the conversational floor, even as multiple speakers overlap or backchannel without taking it. Existing evaluations study dyadic turn-taking or end-to-end agent behavior, but lack a unified, controlled evaluation of genuine floor transitions against confusable non-events in multi-party settings. We introduce MultiPartyTurnBench (MPTB), a benchmark of 240 synthetically generated, channel-separated conversations spanning two to five speakers and six interaction types. MPTB evaluates two complementary tasks: End-of-Turn (EOT) detection distinguishes genuine turn completion from temporary holds, while Interruption (INT) detection distinguishes successful floor takeovers from non-floor-taking speech. Exact event-conditioned annotations enable causal evaluation using false-positive-constrained recall and signed latency. Across acoustic, semantic, and turn-projection baselines, we find a stark asymmetry: learned systems achieve 82.5-92.6% EOT recall at 4.3-11.8% false-positive rates, while INT detection suffers from missed takeovers or excessive false activations. This asymmetry extends to five full-duplex agents which achieve 86.1-95.8% balanced accuracy on turn entry, yet perform near chance (46.9-54.7%) on selective interruption handling. Gemini-3.8-Live yields to 97.7% of backchannels, whereas MiniCPM-o-4.5 yields to only 1.4% of genuine interruptions. These findings establish selective floor control as a distinct, unresolved challenge for reliable multi-party voice interaction.

2610.20179.title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
2610.20179.abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

2610.20193.title: SWE-Stream: Scaling Executable Training Data for SWE Agents via Progressive Construction and Elastic Streaming
2610.20193.abstract: Software engineering agents have advanced rapidly, but scaling their training remains constrained by the limited availability of high-quality executable tasks. Development histories contain valuable signals for constructing such tasks, yet they often require substantial reconstruction due to incomplete environments, missing tests, and inconsistent artifacts. We present SWE-Stream, a system for scaling executable SWE training data through progressive construction and elastic streaming execution. SWE-Stream progressively validates and refines task candidates, reusing existing artifacts when possible and applying targeted completion only when necessary. An elastic scheduler asynchronously coordinates construction stages under shared resource constraints, adapting execution budgets based on observed workload demands. Using development histories from 10,728 repositories across six programming languages, SWE-Stream constructs 80,874 validated tasks and collects 118,688 successful trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on these trajectories achieves resolve rates of 69.0%, 49.3%, and 45.42% on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. In a controlled comparison with approximately matched training budgets, SWE-Stream achieves a 45.6% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming three existing data sources. Moreover, its streaming construction strategy improves efficiency, delivering $1.45\times$ the accepted-task throughput of batch construction and accepting 13.2% more tasks than fixed-limit streaming.

2610.20205.title: What and Where in Identifying and Quantifying Conventions in Humans and AI Agents
2610.20205.abstract: Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1-5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.

2610.20221.title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
2610.20221.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. We introduce a reasoning-guided translation framework for constructing multilingual evaluations designed to preserve the structure and intended meaning of diverse benchmark tasks. Our approach separates translation strategy selection from large-scale generation, combining reasoning-guided configuration selection with task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening. Using this framework, we develop a source-aligned evaluation collection spanning seven safety, conversational, and mathematical reasoning resources across 11 languages. The resulting collection achieves 99.94\% coverage of intended item--language pairs in the two subsets requiring repair. Evaluations of open-source LLMs reveal distinct language-dependent vulnerabilities, including inconsistent refusal behaviour and substantial reasoning degradation in lower-resource languages. These findings highlight the importance of task-sensitive benchmark construction and systematic quality assessment for understanding multilingual model behaviour beyond English.

2610.20243.title: Retrieval Over Training: Similarity search-based Model Selection for Time Series Anomaly Detection
2610.20243.abstract: Anomaly detection is a fundamental task for time-series analytics, with important implications for the downstream performance of many applications. Despite the large number of anomaly detection methods proposed in the literature, recent benchmark studies have shown that no single detector performs best across highly heterogeneous time series. Therefore, a practical and scalable solution is to develop a model-selection method that, for a given time series, selects the anomaly detector most likely to perform well. Nevertheless, the model selection approaches proposed in the literature suffer from a significant drop in accuracy when applied in Out-of-Distribution (OOD) settings. In this paper, we tackle the aforementioned limitation and propose RAMSAD, a retrieval-based framework for model selection in time-series anomaly detection. Given a new time series, our method queries a knowledge base of previously observed instances, retrieves the top-k most similar series, and transfers detector recommendations from their performance profiles. The framework can operate with standard similarity measures as well as embedding-based representations. Our results show that RAMSAD outperforms existing baselines in In-Distribution (ID) settings and is the most robust selector in OOD, where, when selecting a small subset of detectors, it matches or exceeds ensembles that run the entire detector pool, at a fraction of their cost. Overall, we demonstrate that similarity-based retrieval constitutes a strong and efficient foundation for model selection in time-series anomaly detection.

2610.20245.title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
2610.20245.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

2610.20261.title: Harness Policy Distillation: Aligning Agent Policies with Runtime Semantics
2610.20261.abstract: Deploying a general-purpose model as an agent means running it inside a product-specific runtime harness that decides which actions are executable, how state advances, and when the loop may terminate. Ordinary trajectory supervision shows which action was taken but leaves the runtime semantics behind that action implicit. We introduce Harness Policy Distillation (HPD), which makes these runtime control semantics an explicit training target alongside actions to align the harness policy. HPD replays reference trajectories through the harness to recover the runtime semantics that are implicit in ordinary trajectory data, and represents them as control documents at each model-call boundary. These documents provide privileged information for a teacher to generate actions, while harness verification ensures that the resulting targets are executable under the runtime contract. We jointly train a shared model on the runtime semantics recovered from control-state privileged information and native history, thereby internalizing these semantics into the model policy. At deployment, the trained model uses the original harness interface without requiring the control document or any additional supplement. On TRAJECT-Bench with the Pi harness, Qwen3-8B trained with HPD reaches 22.98% autonomous task success and 49.23% runtime compliance, against 3.09% and 19.90% for the unadapted model. Harness-verified teacher actions substantially improve the native deployment policy, while joint control-state supervision provides further gains in task completion and runtime compliance. HPD turns executable runtime semantics into dense supervision for learning harness-compatible actions at each decision boundary.

2610.20264.title: FUSE: Fairness-aware Update Screening against Byzantine Exploitation in $q$-Fair Federated Learning
2610.20264.abstract: Client-level fair federated learning, in the form of $q$-fair federated learning ($q$-FFL), agnostic federated learning, or tilted empirical risk minimization, has emerged as an attractive solution to equalize utility across heterogeneous clients. This paradigm grants high-loss clients greater relative influence, while a central server aggregates their loss-weighted updates into a single shared model. Yet, the Byzantine robustness of $q$-fair federated learning has been largely neglected, leaving the server unable to tell legitimate fairness-induced amplification from malicious update scaling. To address this critical gap, we formalize the problem of Byzantine-robust $q$-fair federated learning under an \emph{update-only interface}, in which the server observes nothing but the fairness-scaled client updates. Our analysis under shared class-conditional label skew shows that fairness scaling preserves the nonnegative class-mixture structure of honest updates, while replacing their unit-sum constraint by a client-dependent radial scale. Moving beyond magnitude-based screening, we show that this warped geometry supplies two complementary tests, one radial and one structural, that a single norm cannot provide. We then introduce FUSE, a structure-aware robust aggregator that uses a small trusted labeled dataset for coefficient recovery, scale and cone-consistency screening, and post-screening step-size control. Across four benchmarks and seven Byzantine attacks, FUSE improves seed-wise worst-attack accuracy over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 3.9--30.1 percentage points, while largely preserving the influence of the high-loss honest clients that fairness is meant to protect.

2610.20272.title: CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing
2610.20272.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code-switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. This context-sensitive ability remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce CSWBench, a benchmark for evaluating context-sensitive code-switching in creative writing through two complementary settings: Focused Narrative and Extended Narrative. We further propose CSWEval, a theory-informed framework with two complementary levels: event-level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole-text evaluation of task-specific quality---overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extended Narrative. Evaluating twelve LLMs, we find that models exhibit meaningful but uneven code-switching competence across narrative contexts. Model differences are particularly pronounced in multilingual literary integration, while multilingual-focused dimensions show stronger difficulty effects overall than the general narrative dimensions; narratively salient switches are associated with stronger contextual and functional realization; and event-level CS quality is moderately associated with whole-text performance.

2610.20347.title: Non-asymptotic Convergence of Average-reward Q-learning with Options
2610.20347.abstract: We study the finite-sample convergence of Q-learning algorithms for the average-reward formulation of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with options. While options allow temporarily extended and hierarchical actions, the average-reward formulation incorporates continual tasks beyond discounted and episodic RL. We establish the first $\tilde{O}(1/\text{iterations})$ convergence guarantees, in the mean-square sense, for average-reward option Q-learning algorithms in both the inter- and intra-option settings. First, we prove that both inter- and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions. Then, we propose synchronous estimators of these multi-step option Bellman operators leading to two variants of option Q-learning. Finally, we extend the stochastic approximation framework to prove convergence rates of these two algorithms under the minimal assumptions used in the literature.

2610.20413.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
2610.20413.abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $\beta$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $\beta$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $\eta$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $\beta$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $\beta$ to keep $\eta/(1-\beta)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $\beta_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

2610.20415.title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM
2610.20415.abstract: Poor generalisation in deep neural networks is frequently associated with convergence to sharp minima. Sharpness-Aware Minimisation (SAM) improves generalisation of deep neural networks by minimising a combination of the training loss and the local sharpness of the loss landscape, biasing convergence towards flat minima. However, SAM relies on a fixed perturbation radius $\rho$ that ignores local curvature, leading to inefficient behaviour: the perturbation may be too small to escape poor basins defined by sharp local minima, or too large to allow convergence to solutions with good loss-sharpness tradeoff. We reinterpret $\rho$ as the intensity of the perturbation signal and propose Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM (CAP-SAM), a geometry-aware method that modulates the perturbation radius based on a sharpness ratio, enabling a more effective search for robust minima on the loss landscape. We prove that CAP-SAM preserves the same convergence rate as standard SAM in non-convex stochastic settings. Extensive experiments indicate that our approach consistently outperforms SAM and its most prominent variants across diverse network architectures on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.

2610.20417.title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
2610.20417.abstract: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03-0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53-0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen's kappa = 0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model-type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency x SC frequency combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6-100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.

2610.20418.title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
2610.20418.abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.

2610.20419.title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
2610.20419.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms. In the realm of LLM, the last two years have seen tremendous progress in RAG architectures, with many models reporting to have improved performance through various design innovations. The cultural question and answering systems of South Asia, in particular, present a specific challenge since the region is home to the vast number of languages and traditions, which are closely interrelated. Along with these deeply intertwined historical narratives increase the need for culturally grounded and context-aware interpretation. Despite major architectural advances in LLMs, claiming significant improvements, challenges remain when answering these region specific questions in native languages. In this study, we aim to extract high-performing factors to guide the development of optimized hybrid RAG systems. We further explore whether the integration of RAG changes performance differently for culturally grounded and non-cultural questions in a South Asian multilingual setup, and whether RAG produces a higher overall percentage of correct answers than contexted answering. We also examine how LLM performance changes when RAG methods are integrated into the question-answering pipeline in comparison with non-contexted and contexted answering and, evaluate whether the introduction of RAG benefits popular or non-popular culturally grounded questions more. Not only does our work evaluate the current methods but also carves a path for future designs of more accurate and efficient question-answering pipelines.

2610.20437.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
2610.20437.abstract: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

2610.20463.title: Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN): An Analysis of Adaptive Action Grids in Decoupled Q-Learning
2610.20463.abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.

2610.20497.title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
2610.20497.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.

2610.20516.title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
2610.20516.abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at this https URL.

2610.20544.title: Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using Convolutional Neural Networks
2610.20544.abstract: Potato is an important food-security crop in Ethiopia, but its production is affected by foliar diseases, particularly early blight and late blight. This study develops a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify potato leaves into three categories: healthy, early blight, and late blight. The proposed model was trained using 2,215 images from the PlantVillage dataset and evaluated on an independent field dataset containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja, Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVillage, the model achieved 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy, and 98.66% test accuracy. On the field dataset, it achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed CNN with VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in terms of classification performance and computational efficiency. The proposed model contains 446,787 trainable parameters, occupies approximately 1.70 MB, and requires an average of 5.58 seconds per training epoch in the reported experimental setup, compared with 9.96 seconds for VGG16 and 7.68 seconds for MobileNetV2. The results demonstrate the potential of a compact CNN for potato leaf disease classification and highlight the importance of independent field evaluation, where image conditions are more variable than in controlled benchmark datasets. The proposed approach may support preliminary disease identification for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and similar agricultural settings.

2610.20548.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
2610.20548.abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

2610.20573.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
2610.20573.abstract: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at this https URL.

2610.20576.title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
2610.20576.abstract: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. We propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), a self-supervised objective that replaces action names with uninformative identifiers and presents each training sample under two interfaces in which equivalent actions are identified by construction. CIPR penalizes the KL divergence between the action distributions induced under the two interfaces, so the policy behaves consistently across them. We evaluate CIPR in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, where it improves robustness. On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce the accuracy of a post-trained agent by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5% while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.

2610.20587.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
2610.20587.abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

2610.20588.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
2610.20588.abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.

2610.15166.title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling
2610.15166.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.

2610.17201.title: Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication
2610.17201.abstract: Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players' perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., $\gamma$-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.

2610.14228.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
2610.14228.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at this https URL.

2610.14544.title: InfraWorld: Motion-Aware World Modeling for Roadside 4D Occupancy Forecasting
2610.14544.abstract: Roadside 4D occupancy forecasting predicts future semantic occupancy in a fixed infrastructure coordinate system. Roadside scenes are globally structured yet locally evolving, requiring comprehensive scene-level context while precisely modeling sparse localized motion. However, existing forecasting paradigms struggle to tackle both requirements. To address this limitation, we propose InfraWorld, a world model formulating roadside occupancy forecasting as selective state evolution. InfraWorld maintains a dense BEV state for the complete scene and persistent motion queries for moving regions, assigning complementary states to global context and local dynamics. Specifically, we propose Dynamic Query Initiation (DQI) to initialize queries in regions supported by motion in the observed history. During rollout, the dense state is updated through Long--Short Temporal Fusion (LST), which combines short-term adjacent-frame continuity with long-term motion trends to preserve stable context while capturing scene evolution. Motion-Aware Query Injection (MAQI) then refines the queries and injects confidence-weighted query information into corresponding BEV tokens, enabling targeted dynamic updates without perturbing global context. Together, InfraWorld concentrates predictive capacity on evolving traffic regions. Extensive experiments on the InfraOcc and Occ3D--nus datasets demonstrate that InfraWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance for roadside 4D occupancy forecasting while retaining its effectiveness under ego-centric settings. Code will be released.

2610.14871.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
2610.14871.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

2610.15343.title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
2610.15343.abstract: World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real-world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object--camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory-aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real-world scenarios. To improve cross-instance optimization compatibility, TARA incorporates trajectory-aware contrastive alignment to encourage attacked representations from diverse video--trajectory instances to approach a shared adversarial region and then performs trajectory-aware task refinement to translate the aligned representation into task-level prediction errors. For reproducible evaluation, we develop a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline that provides physically plausible adversarial regions with temporally consistent trajectories on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Something-Something V2. We further collect real-world print-and-recapture videos to validate attack effectiveness under physical deployment conditions. Together, the annotated benchmarks and real-world captured data form a reproducible testbed for future evaluation. Notably, our results reveal that a single printable adversarial texture can persistently disrupt world models and video understanding models under physical conditions, highlighting the fundamental security challenge.

2610.15562.title: A Plausible Future Is Not a Causal Future: Can Video Models Generate How the World Unfolds?
2610.15562.abstract: Large-scale video generation models are increasingly viewed as a promising path toward world models, yet their ability to capture causally coherent physical dynamics remains poorly understood. Existing evaluations largely emphasize visual quality, prompt adherence, or broad physical plausibility, leaving open whether a model can faithfully realize a complete causal cascade, in which an initiating event propagates through causally dependent interactions to a terminal outcome. We introduce CausalCascade, a simulator-grounded benchmark centered on 50 event-rich Blender scenes with structured event graphs, graph-grounded diagnostic VQA, three levels of future-event specification, and 2,832 controlled counterfactual variants, and use it to evaluate nine image-to-video models with complementary motion-, event-, and counterfactual-level diagnostics. Across the evaluated models, generated motion is more reliably localized spatially than realized with correct spatiotemporal evolution, while richer future-event specification improves event recovery but leaves physical realization limited. Counterfactual evaluation further reveals weak selective responsiveness to physical interventions, while most audited failures are foundational, arising at scene consistency or event occurrence. Together, these results position causal cascade generation as a process-level test of world modeling and highlight the need to jointly recover the intended future, faithfully realize its physical evolution, selectively respond to physical interventions, and maintain a coherent physical world over time. Code and dataset are available at this https URL .

2610.15625.title: 1Step-WAM: Your World Action Model but Faster using 1-Step Action Generation
2610.15625.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify visual world modeling and action generation, yet their real-world deployment is heavily bottlenecked by iterative action denoising and the sequential execution of visual prefilling and action prediction. We demonstrate that the action-denoising trajectories in WAMs are approximately straight, rendering the first-step velocity a strong estimate of the final action direction. Building on this observation, we introduce 1Step-WAM, a framework that transforms multi-step action denoising into one single forward. Specifically, we employ a lightweight calibrator to directly correct the first step velocity, and use bandwidth-constrained action decoding to further reduce errors in the calibrated one-step actions. Compressing action generation into a single step enables it to execute in parallel with visual prefilling, completely breaking the sequential bottleneck of the traditional imagination-then-action paradigm. Evaluations on RoboTwin and LIBERO show that 1Step-WAM largely preserves multi-step task success with only about 13.4M trainable parameters, while achieving inference speedups of $7.44\times$, $5.98\times$, and $24.84\times$ for FastWAM, ImageWAM and Kairos, respectively. Furthermore, real-world robotic deployments using the FastWAM backbone confirm a consistent 7.44$\times$ speedup while maintaining close success rate to the multi-step baseline. Code is avaliable at this https URL.

2610.15645.title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
2610.15645.abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at this https URL.

2610.16166.title: Esports World Model Dataset
2610.16166.abstract: Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly change a shared environment while observing different parts of it. Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires data that connect individual observations and actions to shared state and events. We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours, including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes 4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2 matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views, replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native actions, structured state and events from the same match. The three games expose complementary observation conditions: private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated by teammates and opponents learned from human play.

2610.17141.title: MARS: Systematic Multi-Level Acceleration for World Action Models
2610.17141.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for embodied intelligence by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions. However, their heavy visual encoding and iterative generative inference incur substantial latency, limiting their applicability to high-frequency closed-loop control. Existing training-free acceleration methods typically optimize a single stage, yielding limited speedups or degraded control under aggressive reuse. In this work, we systematically profile the inference overhead of WAMs and observe abundant redundancy across Transformer computation, diffusion denoising, and consecutive policy queries. However, the safe removal of such redundancy depends strongly on its impact on action prediction and control sensitivity. Based on these observations, we introduce \textbf{MARS}, a training-free and plug-and-play framework for multi-level WAM acceleration. MARS selectively removes low-impact attention computation, adaptively accelerates diffusion inference according to motion granularity, and speculatively reuses predicted future visual representations across consecutive queries with online verification. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide remarkable acceleration while limiting approximation error. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa show that MARS achieves up to $4.00\times$, $3.94\times$, and $2.10\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, while maintaining task success rate close to the original policy. Moreover, MARS generalizes across different model backbones and across simulation and real-robot experiments, substantially improving the efficiency--performance trade-off of WAM inference. Our code is available at this https URL.

2610.17434.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
2610.17434.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.

2610.17625.title: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling
2610.17625.abstract: For video generation in dynamic world modeling, observed static and dynamic content should be efficiently reused to provide conditions for repeated generation at different times and viewpoints. We introduce 4LC, a 4D latent cache with composite visual representations and a flexible spatiotemporal access interface. As a latent cache, 4LC directly reuses visual representations of static and dynamic content to provide generation conditions, avoiding per-request RGB rendering and re-encoding. As a composite cache, 4LC binds visual representations from multiple visual encoders (e.g., VAE, DINO, V-JEPA, VGGT) to shared geometry and motion, allowing the composite representations to describe the dynamic world with rich information. Besides, we design a flexible spatiotemporal interface, which directly reads the cache at independently specified times and viewpoints and combines readouts across observations, providing a common conditioning format for diverse downstream tasks. Building on 4LC, we develop 4LC-Video to address multiple video generation tasks through different configurations of source observations, spatiotemporal requests, and historical reuse, including camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation. Our experiments show more efficient condition acquisition, effective spatiotemporal controllability, and scene consistency across tasks using a single 4LC-Video model without task-specific fine-tuning.

2610.17903.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
2610.17903.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.

2610.18305.title: AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
2610.18305.abstract: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely this http URL introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion-Action-World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 233 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define eight metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of five SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos3) required world-state change scores of 0.100-0.280 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states.

2610.14583.title: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon Robotic World Models
2610.14583.abstract: Autoregressive robot video world models based on discrete visual tokens remain unreliable over long rollout horizons. Retaining the entire generated history does not necessarily improve prediction quality. We investigate a possible memory-role conflict in Full Context decoding: persistent scene information, recent visual-action states, and stale generated history compete for attention despite their different predictive roles. This perspective motivates ReCAP (Receding Context with Anchor Preservation), a training-free context-scheduling method for long-horizon robot video world models. ReCAP keeps the pretrained tokenizer, world model, and visual decoder frozen. It preserves the initial scene anchor and a contiguous window of recent complete visual-action blocks while evicting older generated history. The schedule preserves within-block structure and temporal order, requires no additional modules or parameter updates, and bounds active-context growth independently of rollout length. We evaluate ReCAP on RT-1, BridgeV2, LIBERO-90, and CALVIN using frozen autoregressive world models. Across evaluated environments and horizons, ReCAP improves visual fidelity, action-conditioned consistency, and robot structure preservation relative to Full Context. On BridgeV2, it reduces LPIPS by 63.3%. In the system benchmark at H=64, it reduces the logical KV footprint by 73.3% and p50 latency by 6.51%. Attention analyses show increased attention to retained recent states, while history interventions associate larger amounts of stale context with higher prediction error. These observations are consistent with the memory-role-conflict hypothesis, although they do not isolate it from context-length and position-handling effects. Our results support inference-time context scheduling as a practical approach to improving long-horizon robot video prediction and computational efficiency without retraining.

2610.18637.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
2610.18637.abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.

2610.18697.title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models
2610.18697.abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

2610.18826.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions
2610.18826.abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We will release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard.

2610.14186.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
2610.14186.abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.

2610.14727.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
2610.14727.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

2610.16365.title: World Models Need a Physical Registry: Learning Internal Predictive States for Physically Plausible World Models
2610.16365.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: this https URL

2610.16558.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
2610.16558.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.

2610.17059.title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
